claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating has a mixed FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
The baseline coating has a lower density of coherent FCC/BCC phase boundaries than the proposed processed coating.
A high density of coherent FCC/BCC phase boundaries pins dislocations.
Dislocation pinning by coherent FCC/BCC boundaries retards dislocation glide.
Reduced dislocation glide slows progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading.
The relevant creep regime involves dislocation-controlled deformation.
Dislocations are nucleated in both the FCC and BCC regions during continuous loading.
Coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries arrest or deflect dislocations.
Reducing dislocation mobility impedes the accumulation of plastic strain.
Increasing coherent FCC/BCC phase-boundary density lowers the steady-state creep strain rate.
Increasing coherent FCC/BCC phase-boundary density reduces accumulated plastic deformation under otherwise identical loading.
Modifying the cooling rate can increase the density and coherency of FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Minor compositional adjustments can promote stable coherent FCC/BCC interfaces.
The magnitude of creep-resistance improvement depends on the achievable phase-boundary density and on loading and temperature conditions.

contradictions.description: The intervention and experimental design permit compositional adjustments, while the conditions require overall composition to be held constant.

The intervention changes both phase-boundary density and coherency, but the conditions state that all variables other than phase-boundary density are held constant, leaving coherency as an uncontrolled second variable.

The operating conditions and boundary specify constant stress, whereas the falsification experiment specifies constant-load testing; constant load and constant stress are not necessarily equivalent as the specimen deforms.
